near_miss.lead: Infant sprinkling and naming versus Homeric calling of companions
near_miss.why_not: The repeated Norse birth formula has ausinn, participle of ausa, with instrumental vatni. Homeric αὖε and ἤϋσεν mean shouted/called, not drew or poured water. The apparent water-root match is a homograph mapping error; naming is not shared.

Norse sveiti and Greek ἱδρώς are cognate, but the other retrieved root is Norse þolir, a verb of enduring, versus Greek τελαμών, a shield strap. The Norse stanza describes Gríss and a distressed woman, while Homer describes combat equipment and bodily exertion. There is no shared sweat-plus-endure construction.

Norse frost/vind and Latin pruinae/uenti supply two cognate weather terms. Searching Menota found the Finnbogi pair and another literal frost/wind context in NRA-norrfragm-58-C, line 21. The Norse negative coordination describes exposure after shipwreck; Lucretius lists snow, winds, hail, and frost in physical explanation. Neither a fixed binary merism nor a distinctive shared poetic figure is established.

Direct searches of the Homer XML found ἀφυσσάμεθ’ ὕδωρ also at Od. 9.85 and numerous wine-scooping uses. Menota searches found the repeated vatni ausinn birth formula and active infant sprinkling in DG-8-OHleg, line 22. Norse has an infant patient and instrumental water in a naming rite; Homer has water as the object collected by sailors. Cognate material does not establish the same syntax or ritual context.

The Norse impersonal myrkt af nótt describes darkness encountered by a shipwreck survivor. The Vuk corpus confirms the night apostrophe at page 36523 and мрклој ноћи мрака at page 33208, with other conventional dark-night apostrophes. Night/darkness is intrinsically predictable; Norse lacks the Serbian fullness metaphor and the shared syntactic relation. The late Serbian witnesses do not establish inheritance.

The Rybnikov volume has four Легъ ... спать occurrences, including the two anchor lines (23405 and 23519); this is conventional Russian narrative sequencing. Norse liggr locates Sokki nearby with a ship and is not the verb governing an infinitive of sleep. sefr ... um nǽtr describes his habitual sleeping ashore. Three cognate roots therefore do not form the same three-word construction.

The parental nouns are cognate, but the Norse denial of better replacement parents, Sanskrit injunction to regard a teacher as parents, orphan appeal, and Atharvan release of family members are different constructions. The Irish witness describes the deaths of both parents. An ordinary kinship pair alone is insufficient; no distinctive inherited formula is demonstrable.

The Norse seasonal expressions date a conversation and a planned voyage; the Atharvan passages enumerate seasons in protective ritual. Cognate season names do not preserve the same ordered merism, syntax, or function.

near_miss.lead: Placing someone or something on the knee
near_miss.why_not: Norse setr Steinvǫru í kné sér describes carrying a woman on horseback. Sanskrit jānuni āropya introduces breaking a victim’s back or a weapon across the knee. Only the knee noun is securely shared within the relevant construction; the acts and narrative functions differ. Greek land allotment is not a knee scene.

Norse hvíldi with um nóttina describes the two people resting on opposite sides of a partition. Plautus contrasts never being at rest by night or day with future sleep. The Norse passage has no corresponding day/night merism; the association of night and rest is generic.

Raw Menota search found one kné/sleep collocation in the searched short windows, the anchor itself. Raw KUB 36.89 confirms knees (D/L plural) and sleep in Rs. 57′, following Tešimi in Rs. 56′; this is the strongest thematic parallel. However Norse kné is the directional complement of placing the head, followed by an independent inchoative sofnar; Hittite has a locative with a periphrastic sleep predicate. The Norse scene is a trap during grooming, whereas the Hittite invocation recalls divine sleep and calls the storm god to arise. A natural resting posture does not yet exclude independent formation or migrating narrative motif. Moreover the allowed hit.jsonl mapping marks šuppar=iye/a-@schlafen → swep- low confidence: Kloekhorst, EDHIL p. 788, base formation *sup-r-·e/o-, TLHdig derivative mapped at root only. That qualification prevents treating the second cognate as unproblematic. The Latin anchor merely enumerates body parts.

near_miss.lead: Foul smell in personal abuse or anger
near_miss.why_not: Norse fúlt describes the alleged smell from the poet, opposed to the young woman’s fragrance in context. Sanskrit pūti gandhi describes anger as a bitter, hot, foul-smelling draught to be swallowed. There is no shared drinking metaphor in Norse, and only the foulness root is comparable.
